The EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) is defined as the ratio between the incoming power (Pi) and the outgoing power (Po) of an EM wave, given by SE = 10log(Pi/Po) in decibels (dB).

The skin depth (δ) is the depth at which the electric field drops to 1/e of the incident strength and is given by δ = 1/√(πfσμ), where f is the frequency, σ is the electrical conductivity, and μ is the magnetic permeability of the shielding material.

Polymer-based composites with conductive fillers, such as metals, intrinsically conductive polymers, and carbon-based materials, can provide lightweight EMI shielding by combining the advantages of polymers and the conductive fillers.
Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and graphene have higher aspect ratios compared to carbon nanofibers (CNFs) and are more effective in imparting electrical conductivity to polymer matrices for EMI shielding.

Syntactic foams, which are composites with hollow particles embedded in a matrix, can enhance EMI shielding performance through the use of conductive hollow particles, conductive coatings on the hollow particles, or the addition of a second conductive filler in the matrix.
The carbon foam developed by Zhang et al. through direct carbonization of a phthalonitrile-based polymer foam achieved a very high specific EMI shielding effectiveness (SSE) of 341.1 dB cm^3/g.

CNTs/graphene foams offer an alternative to carbon foams for lightweight EMI shielding materials, as they can provide the necessary electrical conductivity without the need for high-temperature carbonization.

In the hybrid epoxy composite foams developed by Xu et al., the highly conductive silver-coated melamine foam (SF) sponge provided channels for rapid electron transport, and the MWCNTs were used to offset the loss of conductive pathways, resulting in a high EMI shielding effectiveness of 68.1 dB.

In the syntactic foams with silver-coated hollow carbon microspheres (Ag-PDA-HCMs) developed by Zhang et al., the contribution of reflection to the EMI shielding effectiveness surpassed that of absorption when the silver content increased to 28.5%.

The specific EMI shielding effectiveness (SSE), defined as the ratio of the EMI shielding effectiveness to the density or to both the density and thickness, is a more appropriate criterion for comparing the EMI shielding performance of materials in applications where lightweight is required.
Electromagnetic (EM) waves are generated when an electric field comes in contact with a magnetic field, and they can travel through anything, including air, water, solid materials, or vacuum.

Electromagnetic interference (EMI) is a disturbance generated by conduction or external radiation that affects an electrical circuit, and it can be encountered in daily life due to the growing number of wireless devices and standards.

Metals, such as galvanized steel and aluminum, have been conventionally used for EMI shielding, but they are disadvantageous in weight consideration, and the EMI signals are almost completely reflected at the surface of the metal, not truly eliminating or mitigating the EMI pollution.

The overall EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) is the sum of the contributions from reflection, absorption, and multiple-reflections, and it depends on the distance between the radiation source and the shielding material.

The effective relative permittivity (ε_eff) of polymer composites, which is one of the most important parameters in the calculation of their EMI shielding effectiveness, can be approximated using the Maxwell Garnett formula.
